title: IEnumerable (sequence interface) and foreach
hook: The foreach loop is not magic — it calls GetEnumerator, then MoveNext and Current in a loop. IEnumerable<T> is the contract that says "you can walk through my items one at a time."

blocks.text: IEnumerable<T> is an interface in System.Collections.Generic that promises a sequence of items. The foreach statement works on any type that provides a GetEnumerator method whose return type has Current and MoveNext. You do not even need to implement IEnumerable<T> directly — if your type has the right pattern, foreach compiles. List<T>, Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, arrays, and yield iterators all support foreach.

entries.plainDefinition: An interface that represents a sequence of items you can walk through one at a time.
entries.example: foreach (Message m in messages) walks an IEnumerable<Message>.

entries.plainDefinition: A cursor object that tracks your position in a sequence. MoveNext advances; Current returns the item at that position.
entries.example: var e = list.GetEnumerator(); e.MoveNext(); var item = e.Current;

entries.plainDefinition: A C# loop that hides the enumerator boilerplate — GetEnumerator, MoveNext, Current, and Dispose.
entries.example: foreach (var x in items) { ... } is syntactic sugar over the enumerator pattern.

entries.plainDefinition: A sequence you can walk and index by position, with a Count property — but not mutate.
entries.example: IReadOnlyList<string> names gives you names[0] and names.Count.

blocks.text: IEnumerable<T> is the most flexible parameter type for methods that only need to walk items. A method accepting IEnumerable<Message> works with a List, an array, a yield iterator, or a LINQ query. The trade-off: IEnumerable<T> does not promise you can Count in O(1) or index by position. Calling Count() on a lazy sequence may enumerate the entire thing. Returning IEnumerable<T> from a public API hides whether you allocated a List or built a deferred iterator.

blocks.title: Walkable, not necessarily materialized
blocks.body: IEnumerable<T> means you can foreach over it. It does not mean the data is already in memory as a list. await foreach on IAsyncEnumerable<T> is a different interface — taught in module 13.

sections.heading: How foreach works step by step

items.title: Get an enumerator
items.body: The compiler calls collection.GetEnumerator() (or an extension method) and stores the result.

items.title: Loop with MoveNext
items.body: while (enumerator.MoveNext()) runs the loop body. MoveNext returns false when there are no more items.

items.title: Read Current
items.body: Inside the loop, the iteration variable is set to enumerator.Current.

items.title: Dispose if needed
items.body: If the enumerator implements IDisposable, foreach calls Dispose when the loop ends — even on an exception.

diagram.title: foreach execution flow
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A[foreach item in collection] --> B[GetEnumerator]
  B --> C{MoveNext?}
  C -->|true| D[item = Current]
  D --> E[Loop body]
  E --> C
  C -->|false| F[Dispose enumerator]
  F --> G[Done]

snippet.label: foreach over any sequence
snippet.explanation: The method accepts any sequence — List, array, or yield iterator. Null throws immediately; an empty sequence simply skips the body.

snippet.label: IEnumerable vs IReadOnlyList
snippet.explanation: Use IEnumerable when you only need to walk. Use IReadOnlyList when callers need Count and an indexer. ICollection and IList add mutation — prefer read-only interfaces on outputs.

blocks.title: Iteration protocols
rows: No boxing (JS has no value types)

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Passing null into foreach and calling it an empty batch — null throws NullReferenceException. Using IEnumerable<T> in a tight inner loop where you needed IReadOnlyList<T> for Count and indexer. Mutating a List while foreach is running — the version counter throws InvalidOperationException.

interviewTakeaways: foreach is MoveNext/Current, plus Dispose when the enumerator is disposable.
IEnumerable<T> is walkable, not necessarily a materialized list.
await foreach / IAsyncEnumerable<T> is module 13, not a foreach flag.
commonPitfalls: Passing a null list into foreach and calling it an empty batch.
Using IEnumerable<T> in a tight inner loop where you needed IReadOnlyList<T> for Count and indexer.

jsTsCorrelations.note: for...of uses Symbol.iterator. C# foreach uses GetEnumerator. Both can be backed by generators/iterators.
TypeScript Iterable<T> is the structural cousin of IEnumerable<T>, erased at run time. IEnumerable<T> is a real CLR interface.
